lines.text: We spent centuries looking up at the stars, asking if we were alone. We imagined vast armadas crossing the dark between worlds. Ancient civilizations, sleeping in the cold hearts of distant galaxies, waiting to be woken. We never considered a simpler truth. The universe does not wage war. It does not conquer. It grows.

Perhaps they traveled across millions of light-years to reach us. Or perhaps... they were never far at all. Woven into the fabric of space itself. Into soil. Into air. Into us. Waiting. Not for an invitation. Just for the right moment to bloom.
There were no sirens. No warnings carved into the sky. Just a silent streak of iridescent fire — tearing through the dark like a dying thought.

When it struck the old lighthouse at Blackwood... it didn't leave ash. It didn't leave ruin. It left something far worse. A seed. Radiant. Patient. Hungry. And the world kept turning — completely unaware that its replacement had already begun.

We call it The Shimmer. A boundary of shifting, oil-slick light slowly swallowing the coastline. It breathes. It expands. And it consumes. It is not destroying our world — it is digesting it. Inside, the laws of physics fracture. Time bleeds. It acts as a prism, refracting every living thing caught within its borders. DNA is pulled apart and stitched back together — a mosaic assembled by hands that have never known mercy.
Military drones don't come back. Animal test subjects don't come back. Twelve human expeditions crossed that threshold. Not one returned intact.
Now, Expedition 13 stands at the edge. Five women. Five fractured lives.
Lena. A cellular biologist haunted by absence. Her husband was the only soul to ever walk out of the Shimmer alive — but whatever came back wearing his face... was not him.

Dr. Ventress. The psychologist who signed the orders that sent eleven teams to their end. A terminal diagnosis has stripped away everything but one final obsession — to reach the source before her body surrenders.

Josie. A physicist who understands the mathematics of existence, yet cannot find her place within it. She looks at the anomaly not with dread, but with the quiet sorrow of someone who has finally found something worth understanding.
Cass. The surveyor. She walks into the nightmare because grief has hollowed her out — the loss of her daughter has made the world outside feel more foreign than any alien wilderness ever could.
And Anya. A paramedic who has built her identity on control, on saving lives, on finding order inside the wreckage. She steps forward into a place that has long since forgotten what life even means.
